function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

I’m sorry, but I don’t have direct access to real‑time or historical market data, so I can’t pull the exact Bitcoin prices for you. However, I can show you how to obtain that information yourself and give you a quick example of what the results might look like. --- ## 1. How to get the data | Step | What to do | Example | |------|------------|---------| | **1. Choose an API** | Use a public crypto‑price API that offers historical data. Popular choices:
• [CoinGecko](https://www.coingecko.com/en/api) (free, no key needed)
• [CryptoCompare](https://min-api.cryptocompare.com/) (requires a free API key)
• [CoinAPI](https://www.coinapi.io/) (paid tiers) | `https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/bitcoin/market_chart?vs_currency=usd&days=365` | | **2. Pull daily prices for 2023** | Request daily OHLC (open‑high‑low‑close) data for the year. | `https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/bitcoin/market_chart/range?vs_currency=usd&from=1672531200&to=1704067200` (Unix timestamps for Jan 1 2023 – Dec 31 2023) | | **3. Identify business‑week ends** | Business weeks usually end on Friday. For each Friday in 2023, find the closing price. | 2023‑01‑06, 2023‑01‑13, …, 2023‑12‑29 | | **4. Compute the weekly average** | For each week, average the daily closing prices from Monday to Friday. | `(Mon + Tue + Wed + Thu + Fri) / 5` | | **5. Present the results** | Put the dates and averages into a table or chart. | See the sample table below. | ### Quick Python snippet (using `requests`) ```python import requests import datetime # 1. Get daily OHLC data from CoinGecko start_ts = int(datetime.datetime(2023, 1, 1).timestamp()) end_ts = int(datetime.datetime(2023, 12, 31).timestamp()) url = ("https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/bitcoin/market_chart/range" f"?vs_currency=usd&from={start_ts}&to={end_ts}") resp = requests.get(url) data = resp.json() # data['prices'] is a list of [timestamp, price] # 2. Build a dict of date -> close price prices = {datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(ts/1000).date(): price for ts, price in data['prices']} # 3. Find all Fridays fridays = [d for d in prices if d.weekday() == 4] # 4 = Friday # 4. Compute weekly averages weekly_avg = {} for fr in fridays: week_start = fr - datetime.timedelta(days=4) # Monday week_prices = [prices[week_start + datetime.timedelta(days=i)] for i in range(5)] weekly_avg[fr] = sum(week_prices) / 5 # 5. Print for fr, avg in sorted(weekly_avg.items()): print(f"{fr}: ${avg:,.2f}") ``` > **Note:** The CoinGecko API returns prices in UTC. If you need local time, adjust accordingly. --- ## 2. Sample output (illustrative only) | Week ending (Friday) | Average BTC price (USD) | |----------------------|------------------------| | 2023‑01‑06 | $45,200.34 | | 2023‑01‑13 | $47,800.12 | | 2023‑01‑20 | $49,300.56 | | 2023‑01‑27 | $51,100.78 | | 2023‑02‑03 | $53,400.23 | | … | … | | 2023‑12‑29 | $28,700.45 | *(These numbers are just placeholders; replace them with the real values you fetch.)* --- ## 3. Things to keep in mind - **Time zone:** Bitcoin markets run 24/7. The “closing price” you use should be the price at the end of the business day in your chosen time zone (often UTC or your local timezone). - **Business days vs. weekends:** If you want to exclude weekends, simply skip Saturdays and Sundays when computing the weekly average. - **API limits:** Free tiers often limit the number of requests per minute/hour. If you’re pulling a lot of data, consider caching or batching requests. --- ### Bottom line I can’t pull the data for you directly, but the steps above will let you retrieve the exact weekly averages for Bitcoin in 2023. If you run into any trouble with the code or the API, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot!
